opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the way I approached his papers changed over time. When I was an undergraduate, I read them the way most students do: I looked at the method and the numbers and thought, "okay, residual connections, that's clever, it works." But as I did more research myself, I started paying attention to something else, which is *how* he picks problems and how he frames them.

What stands out to me is that his papers are almost always very simple at the core. ResNet is basically one idea: let the network learn a residual instead of the full mapping. Momentum Contrast, Masked Autoencoders, it's the same pattern. There's one clean insight, and then everything else in the paper exists to make that insight convincing. Very few tricks, very few knobs. When I first read them I sometimes felt, "is that all?" Later I realized that's exactly the hard part. Finding the one thing that really matters and stripping away everything else takes enormous taste and a lot of failed experiments that never show up in the paper.

So when I study his newer work, I try to ask a few questions. First, what is the bottleneck he thinks the field is stuck on? Usually the paper is a response to some widely held assumption, and if you can identify that assumption, the whole paper suddenly makes sense. Second, what did he deliberately *not* do? Often the restraint tells you as much as the contribution. And third, how does the experimental section build trust? His ablations are very carefully designed so that a skeptical reader runs out of objections.

Another thing I learned is that his writing is part of the research. The figures, the order of the sections, even the title, they're all designed so that a reader walks away remembering one idea. For me as a researcher, that was a big lesson: a result isn't really finished until you can explain it that clearly.

Of course, I'm not saying everyone should do research exactly that way. Some important work is messy and systems-heavy, and that's closer to what I ended up doing later. But reading his papers really shaped my sense of what "good research" looks like: identify the real problem, find the simplest thing that addresses it, and prove it so thoroughly that people just adopt it.

r002.rationale: It discusses why finding a simple idea is hard, but does not ask why He succeeded with ideas students had previously considered.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I had to do was stop trying to read him the way I read most papers. With a lot of work in this field, you skim the abstract, you look at the benchmark table, and you basically know what happened. With Kaiming's papers, the benchmark table is almost the least interesting part. What I learned to do is ask one question: what is the thing he decided not to do?

Take ResNet. Everybody remembers the skip connection, but the real insight is that he looked at a problem everyone else was framing as "deeper networks are harder to optimize, so let's find better optimizers or better initialization," and he reframed it as a representation problem. If the deeper network can't even learn the identity mapping, something is structurally wrong. Once you see that, the residual block is almost obvious. The hard part was asking the right question, not writing the two lines of code.

So when his newer papers come out, I try to find that same move. With MAE, the move was to stop treating images like text. People were copying BERT, masking fifteen percent, and getting mediocre results. He said, images are redundant, mask seventy-five percent, throw away the masked tokens in the encoder entirely, and suddenly it's cheap and it works. Again, the method is simple. The judgment behind it is what's hard to copy.

The other thing I do, and this sounds a bit silly, is I actually reproduce the ablations. His ablation tables are where the thinking lives. He will show you five variations that didn't work, and if you sit with those for an afternoon you understand the paper better than if you read the method section ten times. A lot of his papers are really a story about elimination. Each row in the table is a hypothesis he killed.

And then the last thing is just patience. His papers tend to look underwhelming on the day they drop, and then a year later everybody is building on them. So I've stopped forming an opinion in the first week. I read it, I note what seems too simple, and I come back to it when I'm stuck on something in my own work. Usually that's when it clicks.

r001.rationale: The response says that once the ResNet insight is clear, the residual block is “almost obvious,” and describes the MAE method as simple, conveying that the ideas seem obvious in hindsight.

r002.rationale: The response discusses the judgment behind He’s ideas but does not say students had previously considered similar ideas or ask why He succeeded with them.

astra-6.text: I’d start by trying to understand the problem he was addressing. What wasn’t working well in existing approaches, and what was the central idea behind the new paper? Then I’d go through the method and experiments to see how they supported that idea. If something wasn’t clear, I’d go back to the earlier papers it built on. The goal was to understand why the approach made sense, rather than just follow the technical details.
